name: Computer matchmaking
definition: A computer that pairs people as romantic partners or spouses by comparing their recorded traits.

first_pass.what: Operation Match, run by Harvard students through Compatibility Research Inc., matched people from questionnaire answers punched onto cards and run on an IBM computer. The search summary says a London service, St. James Computer Dating Service, began in 1964.

first_pass_note: Mass adoption not established; Operation Match reached over a million respondents by 1968.

name: Computerized personnel selection and aptitude testing
definition: Computers that test aptitude and personality and choose people for jobs, schools or missions from their records.

first_pass.what: The US Department of Defense began operational use of the computerized adaptive ASVAB (CAT-ASVAB) at Military Entrance Processing Stations in 1996-1997. This is a loose fit: it tests aptitude by computer but does not choose from records.

first_pass_note: Loose fit: CAT-ASVAB tests aptitude by computer. Project TALENT was paper-based.
doubt: 1996 CAT-ASVAB is late; computerized test scoring/selection is much older.

name: Computerized courts and legal decisions
definition: Computers that decide verdicts or sentences, issue warrants or do legal research in place of judges and lawyers.

first_pass.what: Mead Data Central launched the LEXIS computerized legal research service commercially, with four big firms as first subscribers. It carried Ohio and New York codes and cases, the US Code and some federal case law.

first_pass_note: Only the legal research part is real; no computer decides verdicts or sentences.

name: Computer crime detection and predictive policing
definition: Computers that analyse police records and evidence to identify suspects or predict where crime will happen.

first_pass.what: The LAPD deployed PredPol, a UCLA-developed algorithm for predicting where crime will happen, in its Foothill Division in late 2011. Santa Cruz also began trying it in 2011.

first_pass_note: Predictive policing found for 2011. NCIC (1967) was not verified.
doubt: 2011 PredPol is late if earlier computerized crime detection (NCIC 1967, crime-pattern computers) fits the definition.

name: Electronic voting and vote counting
definition: Votes cast or counted by electrical or computer machines, with totals reported automatically.

first_pass.what: Georgia counties were the first to use punch cards and computer tally machines for voting, per a timeline source. The Votomatic punch-card system was introduced around 1964. The exact county and year are unconfirmed.

first_pass_note: Lever machines (1892) are mechanical, so left out. Punch-card computer tally 1964 is only a timeline-level source.

name: Central citizen database and mass surveillance
definition: A government computer that holds a dossier on every citizen and tracks them through their records.
first_pass_note: No milestone. The Stasi central file was a card index, and Swedish registers were not a dossier on each citizen.
doubt: Refused in first pass; check whether a central computerized citizen database fits.

name: Automated eavesdropping
definition: Machines that record, transcribe and screen phone calls and conversations to find crime or dissent.
first_pass_note: No milestone. SHAMROCK handled telegrams largely by hand, and I found no source for automated speech screening.

name: Electronic location tracking of people
definition: Worn tags, implants or devices that report where a person or vehicle is to a monitoring system.

first_pass.what: Ralph Schwitzgebel and his brother Robert, at Harvard, built a system that relayed signals from worn transmitters to a surplus missile-tracking device and displayed participants' positions on a large screen. The start date is uncertain.

Judge Jack Love in New Mexico ordered a Michael Goss radio-frequency ankle transmitter attached to a probation violator for a month. This was radio-based, not GPS; GPS offender monitoring was piloted in Florida in 1997.

first_pass_note: The 1983 tag was radio-based; GPS offender monitoring was piloted in 1997.

name: Machine-readable identity and access card
definition: A card, disc or token encoded with a person's identity that machines read to grant access or check identity.

first_pass.what: IBM engineer Forrest Parry made the first prototype of a plastic card with magnetic tape, meant as a secure ID card for CIA officials. The year is uncertain.
Tor Sørnes launched the VingCard, the first recodable cardkey lock, using a punched-hole plastic key. A hotel that had suffered burglaries tested it. The date comes from a single source.

first_pass_note: IBM's first magstripe field test was January 1970 at O'Hare (a transaction card); magstripe hotel locks came in 1992-93.

name: Automated fingerprint recognition
definition: A machine that identifies or authenticates a person by automatically reading and matching fingerprints.

first_pass.what: The FBI's IAFIS, built by Lockheed Martin, became operational in July 1999. It is not the earliest automated system: the FBI began its automation effort around 1969 and had Rockwell build the first AFIS card readers. I could not confirm that date.

first_pass_note: Earliest automated systems (Mitre Identimat 1961, FBI-Rockwell 1970s) were not confirmed; 1999 IAFIS is the best-sourced date.
doubt: 1999 FBI IAFIS is a national database, the wrong kind of event for a fingerprint lock or reader; earlier automated systems (e.g. Identimat hand geometry 1960s/70s, FBI/Rockwell automated readers 1970s, fingerprint access control) were never checked. Probably decades late.

name: Retina and iris recognition
definition: A machine that identifies a person by scanning the patterns of the eye.

first_pass.what: John Daugman was awarded a patent for his automated iris recognition algorithms. Flom and Safir had patented the concept of iris identification in 1986 or 1987. The retina-scanning half of the concept was not covered by my searches.
The FBI's iris recognition overview says the first commercial iris recognition products became available in 1995. Iris ID dates its commercially viable IrisAccess 2200 to 1999.

first_pass_note: Only iris covered; retina scanning (EyeDentify) not confirmed.
doubt: Only iris covered; commercial retina scanners (EyeDentify, late 1970s/early 1980s) are older than the 1995 iris product. Probably late.

name: Automated face recognition
definition: Cameras and computers that identify people by matching their faces against stored images.

first_pass.what: Woody Bledsoe, Helen Chan and Charles Bisson worked in 1964-65 on semi-automated computer recognition of faces. This was semi-automated; Kanade's 1973 system is sometimes called the first fully automated one.

first_pass_note: Practical use (e.g., Super Bowl XXXV 2001) not searched.

name: Voiceprint speaker recognition
definition: A machine that identifies or authenticates a person by the pattern of their voice.

first_pass.what: Pruzansky and Mathews at Bell Labs published early speaker recognition experiments on ten talkers. Doddington at Texas Instruments built a speaker verification system in the early 1970s.

first_pass_note: Practical use date not confirmed; TI system in the early 1970s was a lab system.

name: Office automation
definition: Computers and machines that do clerical work such as correspondence, filing, billing and payroll.

first_pass.what: LEO I at J. Lyons & Co. ran the first business application, bakery valuations, on 5 September 1951. One source says it first did payroll in November 1951; another says regular payroll began in December 1953. IBM introduced the MT/ST in 1964, which popularised the term word processing.

name: Society's dependence on fallible computers
definition: A society that treats computer records and judgments as infallible and suffers when they are wrong or fail.
first_pass_note: A social condition, not a device; no dated milestone given.
